summary: Windmill Point Light, where the Detroit River meets Lake St. Clair: lit 1838, rebuilt 1875 and again 1933, with keepers' rescues in the 1910s and 1920s; Coast Guard-owned, tower closed.

lens.note: Sixth-order lens in the lower lantern of the 1933 tower (LighthouseFriends, quoting the Bulletin).

structures.type: octagonal concrete base with cylindrical steel tower
structures.note: Steel tower about 33 ft above its concrete base (LighthouseFriends, quoting the Bulletin).

structures.type: ten-room brick keepers dwelling, doubled in 1908

access.note: Grounds open at Mariner Park; tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Congress appropriates $5,000 for a light on Windmill Island at the outlet of Lake St. Clair (LighthouseFriends).
Light placed in operation (LighthouseFriends). Keeper John M. Martin from 1838 (USLHS).
Larger fifth-order lens: fixed white varied by a red flash every ninety seconds (LighthouseFriends).
New conical brick tower and dwelling, begun May 1875, finished October 1875 (LighthouseFriends). Height: 57 ft per LighthouseFriends; 51 ft tower and 55 ft focal height per USLHS.
Fourth-order lens; on 7 December 1890 the light became a fixed white varied by a red flash every fifteen seconds (Board report, fiscal year ended 1891; LighthouseFriends).
Range lights authorized 3 March 1891 ($3,000), exhibited 20 May 1891; first assistant keeper appointed (Board report; LighthouseFriends).
Wooden range towers replaced by two steel towers (LighthouseFriends).
Eight rooms added to the dwelling to make a double dwelling (LighthouseFriends).
Marshall and his assistant pulled a boat near the seawall to safety in heavy seas (LighthouseFriends).
Two keepers towed a disabled boat to shore; Marshall rescued a man from drowning (LighthouseFriends).
Front range tower raised 15 ft and rear tower 20 ft; electric lights installed in the dwelling, range lights and lighthouse (LighthouseFriends).
Redman and Story rescued four men whose boat had capsized (Commissioner, fiscal year ended 30 June 1921).
Redman and Story rescued two persons who had become exhausted (Commissioner, fiscal year ended 30 June 1922).
Range lights discontinued; towers moved to the St. Marys River (LighthouseFriends).
New light commenced operation 1 April 1933 (LighthouseFriends; Bulletin heading 1934).
Old 1875 tower torn down after the new light began (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive flags the station as not existing, but the standing 1933 tower and the grounds are described by LighthouseFriends, and the 1934 Bulletin records the new light. The record's "standing" status is kept; the archive flag is treated as out of date.
The 1933 date is confirmed by LighthouseFriends (commenced 1 April 1933) and by the Bulletin note headed New Windmill Point Light.

Not resolved. LighthouseFriends gives the tower as nearly fifty-seven feet; the USLHS place record gives 51 feet from base to lantern centre and 55 feet focal height. The story states the disagreement.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the first stone tower stood nearly forty-four feet (about 13.4 m). The record's 12.0 m is not sourced in the material read.

notes_for_editor:
Keeper roster: 29 lines from the USLHS archive (1838-1930), matched by name and position (0.55 km). Walter G. Marshall's Spectacle Reef service is LighthouseFriends' statement; the other_stations entry has no id on the map beyond the Spectacle Reef record (us-mi-spectacle-reef, which exists in data/stations).
Conflicts left open: (1) first tower height (record 12.0 m; LighthouseFriends nearly 44 ft); (2) 1875 tower height (LighthouseFriends nearly 57 ft; USLHS 51 ft tower and 55 ft focal height); (3) focal height in the record (Wikidata 13.0, OSM 12.8, USLHS 16.76 m) not resolved; (4) Charles H. Haven 1927-1930 (USLHS) vs 1927-1929 (LighthouseFriends).
Mattie Kennedy: the archive lists her as acting principal keeper for 1907; LighthouseFriends lists "Mattie Kennedy (1907)" as head keeper. The sources read do not give her relationship to Nathan James Roach Kennedy. A Chronicling America search for 1907 found nothing relevant.
Rescues 1915 and 1916 (Marshall): LighthouseFriends only. The Commissioner's fiscal 1916 and 1917 "vessels aided" tables name W. G. Marshall at Windmill Point, but the OCR separates vessel names from keepers, so no vessel is tied to him there; not used.
The 1933 tower description is LighthouseFriends quoting the Bulletin; the Bulletin page is OCR-jumbled, so only its heading is quoted.
Characteristic: the Board report and LighthouseFriends agree on the 1890 change to a red flash every fifteen seconds. The current characteristic in the record (Iso W 6s, from the Light List) was not checked.
The USLHS place record says "Existing: No" and "Active AtoN: No", which conflicts with the standing light; flagged as out of date in resolved_conflicts.
Ownership: LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard owns the light. No other ownership source read.
Wikipedia lead gives the 1837 appropriation and John Martin as first keeper, consistent with LighthouseFriends; not cited.
Printed pages not read: Internet Archive citations use scan pages (the 1891 report page 200; the 1921 and 1922 Commissioner pages 667 and 756). Check the page images before printing a page number.
No photos mirrored: LighthouseFriends photographs are copyrighted.
Verification 2026-10-27: story now states the 1875 tower-height disagreement and that the archive's place record marks the station not open to the public; 'first appropriation' and the 'guide' wording and the 1867 characteristic were corrected; Mattie Kennedy's LighthouseFriends listing is noted. Checked the 1891 Board report (scan 200 is FY1891: the volume's FY1892 header is at the text position after 'range lights' entries), the 1921/1922 Commissioner rescues (scan 667 and 756 sit under the FISCAL YEAR 1921 and 1922 headers), and the 1934 Bulletin heading (PDF p. 27, OCR). The 1915-1917 Commissioner 'aided' tables were checked: each keeper's name is followed by its station, so Marshall and McFall are at Windmill Point in 1915-1917; those tables were not cited because the vessel column cannot be tied to them. Putnam was not used for this station.
